    NIS-FRVM Survey Demo¶

    This notebook fits a vaxflux model to real flu vaccination coverage data from the CDC's National Immunization Survey (NIS-FluVaxView / FRVM), covering five seasons and three age groups. Unlike the synthetic demos, the data and season structure come directly from the survey, so this is closer to what a real analysis workflow looks like.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import arviz as az
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpyro
import pandas as pd

from vaxflux import (
    CovariateCategories,
    LogisticCurve,
    PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate,
    SeasonRange,
    SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate,
    VaxfluxModel,
    VaxfluxObservations,
)
from vaxflux.data import get_ncird_nis_frvm_flu_vaccination_coverage

numpyro.set_host_device_count(8)
az.style.use("arviz-docgrid")
    import arviz as az import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpyro import pandas as pd from vaxflux import ( CovariateCategories, LogisticCurve, PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate, SeasonRange, SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate, VaxfluxModel, VaxfluxObservations, ) from vaxflux.data import get_ncird_nis_frvm_flu_vaccination_coverage numpyro.set_host_device_count(8) az.style.use("arviz-docgrid")

    Load Real Survey Data¶

    get_ncird_nis_frvm_flu_vaccination_coverage fetches CDC NIS-FRVM flu vaccination coverage estimates. Passing include_age_groups=True returns data stratified by age group (18–49, 50–64, 65+). The result is wrapped in VaxfluxObservations. Displaying the head confirms the expected long-form structure: one row per (season, age, time window) with an incidence value.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    observations = VaxfluxObservations.from_dataframe(
    get_ncird_nis_frvm_flu_vaccination_coverage(include_age_groups=True)
)
observations.data.head()

    Inspect Total Season Prevalence¶

    A quick sanity check: summing incidence within each (season, age) group gives cumulative season prevalence — the total vaccination coverage by season end. The 65+ group consistently shows the highest coverage (~65–72%), as expected for flu vaccination.

    Plot the Observed Data¶

    A visual overview of the NIS-FRVM data. The top panel shows bi-weekly incidence (new vaccinations) and the bottom shows cumulative prevalence, broken out by season and age group. The early-season surge pattern and age-group ordering are clearly visible.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    plot_data = observations.data.copy()
plot_data["start_date"] = pd.to_datetime(plot_data["start_date"])
plot_data["end_date"] = pd.to_datetime(plot_data["end_date"])
plot_data["mid_date"] = (
    plot_data["start_date"] + (plot_data["end_date"] - plot_data["start_date"]) / 2
)
plot_data = plot_data.sort_values("mid_date")
plot_data["prevalence"] = plot_data.groupby(["season", "age"])["value"].cumsum()

fig, (ax_inc, ax_prev) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 8), sharex=True)

for (season, age), group in plot_data.groupby(["season", "age"]):
    label = f"{season} | {age}"
    ax_inc.plot(group["mid_date"], group["value"], label=label)
    ax_prev.plot(group["mid_date"], group["prevalence"], label=label)

ax_inc.set_title("Sample observations by season and age")
ax_inc.set_ylabel("Incidence")

ax_prev.set_title("Cumulative prevalence by season and age")
ax_prev.set_ylabel("Prevalence")
ax_prev.set_xlabel("Date")

fig.legend(handles, labels, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5))
for label in ax_prev.get_xticklabels():
    label.set_rotation(30)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 0.85, 1))
plt.show()

    Instantiate the Logistic Curve¶

    LogisticCurve is the functional form used to model vaccination uptake over time within a season.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    curve = LogisticCurve()
curve
    curve = LogisticCurve() curve
    Out[5]:
    $$f(t \mid m, r, s) = \operatorname{expit}(m)\operatorname{expit}\left(e^r(t-s)\right)$$

    Extract Season Ranges and Age Categories from the Data¶

    Rather than hardcoding season boundaries, we derive SeasonRange objects directly from the observations data. Similarly, age categories are extracted from the unique values in the age column. This keeps the model setup in sync with whatever the data actually contains.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    season_bounds = (
    observations.data.groupby("season", as_index=False)
    .agg(
        season_start_date=("season_start_date", "min"),
        season_end_date=("season_end_date", "max"),
    )
    .sort_values("season")
)
seasons = [
    SeasonRange(
        season=row.season,
        start_date=row.season_start_date.date(),
        end_date=row.season_end_date.date(),
    )
    for row in season_bounds.itertuples(index=False)
]

age_covariate_categories = CovariateCategories(
    covariate="age",
    categories=tuple(observations.data["age"].drop_duplicates().tolist()),
)
    season_bounds = ( observations.data.groupby("season", as_index=False) .agg( season_start_date=("season_start_date", "min"), season_end_date=("season_end_date", "max"), ) .sort_values("season") ) seasons = [ SeasonRange( season=row.season, start_date=row.season_start_date.date(), end_date=row.season_end_date.date(), ) for row in season_bounds.itertuples(index=False) ] age_covariate_categories = CovariateCategories( covariate="age", categories=tuple(observations.data["age"].drop_duplicates().tolist()), )

    Define Prior Covariates¶

    Priors are specified for all three logistic curve parameters (m, r, s) at the season level, plus season-varying age offsets for all three parameters. The tighter sigma values here (compared to the synthetic demo) reflect that the NIS-FRVM data is real and the priors should be more constrained around known vaccination patterns.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    covariates = [
    PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate(
        parameter="m",
        covariate=None,
        mu_mu=-0.5,
        mu_sigma=0.5,
        sigma=0.5,
    ),
    PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate(
        parameter="r",
        covariate=None,
        mu_mu=-3.5,
        mu_sigma=0.5,
        sigma=0.5,
    ),
    PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate(
        parameter="s",
        covariate=None,
        mu_mu=60.0,
        mu_sigma=10.0,
        sigma=10.0,
    ),
    SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate(
        parameter="m",
        covariate="age",
        mu_mu=1.5,
        mu_sigma=0.5,
        sigma=0.5,
    ),
    SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate(
        parameter="r",
        covariate="age",
        mu_mu=0.5,
        mu_sigma=0.5,
        sigma=0.5,
    ),
    SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate(
        parameter="s",
        covariate="age",
        mu_mu=0.0,
        mu_sigma=10.0,
        sigma=10.0,
    ),
]
    covariates = [ PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate( parameter="m", covariate=None, mu_mu=-0.5, mu_sigma=0.5, sigma=0.5, ), PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate( parameter="r", covariate=None, mu_mu=-3.5, mu_sigma=0.5, sigma=0.5, ), PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate( parameter="s", covariate=None, mu_mu=60.0, mu_sigma=10.0, sigma=10.0, ), SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate( parameter="m", covariate="age", mu_mu=1.5, mu_sigma=0.5, sigma=0.5, ), SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate( parameter="r", covariate="age", mu_mu=0.5, mu_sigma=0.5, sigma=0.5, ), SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate( parameter="s", covariate="age", mu_mu=0.0, mu_sigma=10.0, sigma=10.0, ), ]

    Build the Model¶

    The model is assembled without .add_dates because the NIS-FRVM data has non-uniform reporting intervals (bi-weekly, monthly), so dates come directly from the observations rather than being generated by daily_date_ranges. A slightly larger observation noise (noise=0.01) is used compared to the synthetic demos, since real survey data carries measurement error.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    model = (
    VaxfluxModel(curve=curve)
    .add_seasons(seasons)
    .add_covariate_categories(age_covariate_categories)
    .add_covariates(covariates)
    .add_observations(observations)
    .add_observation_process(
        kind="normal",
        noise=0.01,
    )
)
model
    model = ( VaxfluxModel(curve=curve) .add_seasons(seasons) .add_covariate_categories(age_covariate_categories) .add_covariates(covariates) .add_observations(observations) .add_observation_process( kind="normal", noise=0.01, ) ) model

    Run Prior Predictive Sampling¶

    Draw 100 samples from the prior to perform a prior predictive check before conditioning on the real data.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    prior_samples = 100
vaxflux_prior_idata = model.sample(samples=None, prior_samples=prior_samples)
vaxflux_prior_idata
    prior_samples = 100 vaxflux_prior_idata = model.sample(samples=None, prior_samples=prior_samples) vaxflux_prior_idata

    Inspect Prior Predictive Observations¶

    Browse the prior predictive draws in long-form to get a sense of the range of incidence values the prior generates. These should look qualitatively similar to the observed data.

    Plot Prior Predictive Curves¶

    Visual prior predictive check: the band of prior draws should envelope the observed data while being sufficiently broad to reflect prior uncertainty.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    vaxflux_prior_idata.plot_prior_predictive()
plt.show()
    vaxflux_prior_idata.plot_prior_predictive() plt.show()

    Run MCMC Posterior Sampling¶

    Run NUTS with 2 chains, 250 warmup steps, and 250 posterior draws. More samples than the synthetic demos are used here given the greater complexity of fitting real data across 5 seasons and 3 age groups.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    warmup = 250
samples = 250
chains = 2
vaxflux_idata = model.sample(
    warmup=warmup, samples=samples, prior_samples=None, chains=chains
)
vaxflux_idata
    warmup = 250 samples = 250 chains = 2 vaxflux_idata = model.sample( warmup=warmup, samples=samples, prior_samples=None, chains=chains ) vaxflux_idata
      0%|          | 0/500 [00:00<?, ?it/s]
      0%|          | 0/500 [00:00<?, ?it/s]

    Inspect Posterior Observations¶

    Browse the posterior predictive draws. For real data, these should cluster tightly around the observed values if the model fits well.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    vaxflux_idata.posterior_observations
    vaxflux_idata.posterior_observations

    Trace Plots for Convergence Diagnostics¶

    Check MCMC chain convergence. With real data the parameter space is more complex — all three curve parameters have both season-level and age-level components — so trace plots are especially important for catching any chain mixing issues.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    az.plot_trace(
    vaxflux_idata,
    var_names=[
        "m_age",
        "m_age_mu",
        "m_age_sigma",
        "r_age",
        "r_age_mu",
        "r_age_sigma",
        "s_age",
        "s_age_mu",
        "s_age_sigma",
        "m_season",
        "m_season_mu",
        "m_season_sigma",
        "r_season",
        "r_season_mu",
        "r_season_sigma",
        "s_season",
        "s_season_mu",
        "s_season_sigma",
        "observation_sigma",
    ],
)
plt.show()
    az.plot_trace( vaxflux_idata, var_names=[ "m_age", "m_age_mu", "m_age_sigma", "r_age", "r_age_mu", "r_age_sigma", "s_age", "s_age_mu", "s_age_sigma", "m_season", "m_season_mu", "m_season_sigma", "r_season", "r_season_mu", "r_season_sigma", "s_season", "s_season_mu", "s_season_sigma", "observation_sigma", ], ) plt.show()

    Plot Posterior Predictive Fit¶

    Overlay the posterior credible interval on the observed data. A well-fitting model should show the data within the posterior band with a narrow uncertainty region.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    vaxflux_idata.plot_posterior_predictive()
plt.show()
    vaxflux_idata.plot_posterior_predictive() plt.show()

    Plot Posterior Predictive with Observation Noise¶

    Including observation noise gives the full predictive distribution — the range of incidence values the model expects to see in future surveys, accounting for both parameter uncertainty and measurement noise.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    vaxflux_idata.plot_posterior_predictive(predictive="observation")
plt.show()
    vaxflux_idata.plot_posterior_predictive(predictive="observation") plt.show()

    Summarize Posterior Prevalence Scenarios¶

    posterior_prevalence_scenarios reports the model's posterior estimates of season-end vaccination coverage, broken out by season and age group. These quantile bands ("low", "typical", "high") summarize how much of the population was vaccinated by the end of each season according to the fitted model.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    vaxflux_idata.posterior_prevalence_scenarios(
    scenarios={"low": (0.05, 0.3), "typical": (0.3, 0.7), "high": (0.7, 0.95)}
)
    vaxflux_idata.posterior_prevalence_scenarios( scenarios={"low": (0.05, 0.3), "typical": (0.3, 0.7), "high": (0.7, 0.95)} )
    In [ ]:
